title: What's the Point of a Consequence?
author: Debbie
summary: Writing under the byline Debbie at the Shift Happens newsletter, this piece reframes classroom consequences around a single question teachers should ask before acting: what is the goal? The author, a former alternative urban middle school teacher, argues that consequences work best when they hold students accountable without foreclosing their ability to repair the situation. She warns against codifying rigid, pre-written consequence policies because they strip teachers of the judgment needed to account for thirty different students' circumstances, and she recommends deferring heated disputes ("we can talk about it after class") to keep one bad choice from escalating into a public standoff. The piece closes on the idea that a consequence should always leave the student a way back rather than trapping them in failure.
points: Debbie argues the real diagnostic question before assigning any consequence is not what the student did wrong but what outcome the teacher is actually trying to produce.
She recommends against writing specific consequences into policy in advance, since rigid rules remove the flexibility teachers need to respond to each student's individual circumstances.
Deferring an in-the-moment argument over a consequence keeps a single infraction from becoming a public power struggle that derails the room.
The piece's central claim is that a consequence should hold a student accountable while still leaving them a visible path back, rather than convincing them nothing they do now matters.
quotes: But before deciding what the consequence should be, there is a question we do not ask often enough: What is your goal? Are you trying to punish the student for what they did, or can the consequence become an opportunity to help change what happens the next time?

One thing I would avoid is putting specific consequences in writing. Thirty students bring a lot of variables with them, and the more specific you are about exactly what will happen, the less room you have to take those variables into account.

A harsh consequence can create a domino effect in the classroom. It starts with, "That's not fair," and before long you are debating the consequence in front of everyone instead of dealing with the behavior that started it.
That gives you time to think. It gives the student time too. Most importantly, it keeps one bad choice from turning into a much bigger problem in front of the class.
A consequence should hold a student accountable without trapping them in the failure. There still needs to be something they can do next that improves the situation.
The point of a consequence is not simply to make a student pay for a mistake. It is to help make a different choice more likely the next time.
